en: The importance of the euro for economic and financial policy in Europe was laid down by Dr. Willem F. Duisenberg, President of the European Central Bank, at the 1998 forecast-for-profit forum, on 23 October 1998 in Basel Introduction In good two months, eleven European states will jointly implement a historic project. They will be replaced by a single currency - the euro. From 1 January 1999, the exchange rate between the currencies of the eleven participating countries will be fixed irrevocably. At the same time, the responsibility for monetary policy in the euro area in the euro area will be applied to the European Central Bank, the euro area of central banks (the euro4ZB) will be replaced by their national currency. The introduction of a single currency will undoubtedly have a wide range of economic consequences, although not only in the participating countries but also in the global trading system. However, it is also an important symbolic step in the long way towards European integration. In my present speech, I am going to focus on the importance of the introduction of the euro from three different perspectives. I will next consider how the introduction of the euro into the economic scenario in the participating countries will affect the euro. The EESC's establishment determines that the primary objective of the single European monetary policy is to restore price stability within the euro area as a whole. This means that the ESF's monetary policy in areas where a Member State has an event to pay, which has no or only limited effects on the other euro area (the so-called ‘aasymmetric shock’), has no room to react in a different way. The necessary adjustment is therefore carried out by means of other policy options, which are not limited to the other euro area (the so-called ‘aisymmetric shock’). However, since the active use of this policy instrument is generally more expensive than it is, it is a short-term instrument which has been used as a necessity instead of the underlying structural problems of the economy. The economy is mainly dependent on regular savings, which, within a short period of time on reassessment, speculative attacks, less credibility and higher interest rates. These structural problems were precisely the growth perspectives of many European countries and the unemployment increased at a high level. I am of the view that this was a very important positive effect of the convergence process of the noted consensus, which was under the policy framework and also in the broad public policy of the pursuit of sound macroeconomic policy, which means that money policy is primarily on the long-term management of the economy and the long-term policy of employment. In fact, inflation rates and interest rates are not only stated, they are even at a level that is to be referred to as a historical period. At the same time, the exchange rate of the Member States' currencies is a long period of time in the vicinity of the respective countries of the exchange rate mechanism, which has remained stable. The positive effects of this process are clearly seen in the wake of the most recent crisis on the financial markets. The exchange rate and interest rate remain largely unchanged throughout the euro area itself, as the turbulence were the most important. This can be interpreted as a sign of market participants' confidence in the euro. However, we cannot afford it, in our convergence approaches, as soon as the changeover has been made. In order to ensure that the exchange rate and interest rate remain largely unchanged, it is necessary to ensure that the exchange rate of the euro area is maintained and that the interest rate of the euro is maintained. In June 1997, the European Council, as it decided on the so-called Stability and Growth Pact, decided that a strong macro-economic policy could also be maintained if the euro area should be affected by an economic downturn. In fact, the strict implementation of the objectives of the Stability and Growth Pact is an essential prerequisite for the restoration of a financial policy area. In recent decades, it has been possible for automatic stabilizationists throughout Europe to be able to take their full action. This was particularly evident at the beginning of the 1990s when some countries were forced to pursue a pro-cyclical policy because of the need to rebuild confidence in financial policy. The high level of public debt is concerned, particularly in view of the long-term challenges facing people in Europe. The debt in the euro area is therefore significantly reduced, before the financial policy instrument can be used effectively again. The medium-term objective of the Stability and Growth Pact, which is closely linked to the recognition of progress towards the stabilization of policies and the high level of action, is also to create an area of action to enable automatic stabilisers to achieve economic recovery, without the challenges of public households to increase the ceiling of 3% of GDP. The monetary policy is neither the cause nor the solution of this problem. Unemployment can only be overcome by structural reforms aimed at making labour markets more efficient. I believe this conclusion is on hand when compared with the countries of Europe. In those countries which have already implemented structural reforms to increase flexibility in the labour markets, unemployment is much stronger than in those in which such reforms are still being made. The impact on the business area in Europe is possible, since the economic consequences of the introduction of the euro in order to improve the long-term growth potential and thus the employment prospects of the countries involved in the euro area are even more important than the macroeconomic ones. However, it may be even more important that the loss of the exchange rate risks is linked to long-term, cross-border investments within the euro area. Other benefits are less obvious. For example, the fact that the same currency is used alone, encourages small and medium-sized enterprises with limited experience in dealing with foreign currencies to take the step in new markets within the euro area. This would result in increased competition within the euro area. The introduction of a single currency is likely to result in price differences and a further rise for both consumers and customers to seek more customers in a neighbouring country. Together all these factors will be used to promote the European internal market for goods and services. In addition, companies will be offered an increase, within the euro area and through mergers and acquisitions. In this context, the effects of the introduction of the euro are likely to occur in the most significant and rapid part of the financial sector. The euro - The effects on the financial markets in Europe The effects of the introduction of the euro on the financial markets are directly linked to the activities of the ESF, which will be the case in other sectors. The interest rates within the euro area as a whole reflect in particular the different risk of solvency between participating banks as a country-specific factor. Secondly, in order to promote the development of an integrated monetary market, the ESF has a market-oriented framework for the implementation of the single currency policy. Regular, updated pensions, which are given in the tendering procedure, will have a particularly large impact. The development of the instruments for pensioned businesses is likely to increase the amount of time spent on the euro area and reduce the amount of time spent on pensions. Thirdly, the ESRB will also use a minimum reserve system for the stabilization of the cash market and the extension of the structural deficit in the banking sector, where I am concerned, because the ESRB has set a special value in the establishment of the minimum reserve system, since it is compatible with the market base. For example, the minimum reserves are subject to the most important rate of refinancing of the ETSB, and the minimum duty is calculated according to the average rate of the investments, since they are to be fixed at the end of a monthly minimum period of time. In addition, its business partners will have the possibility of cross-border security within the euro area. This approach is likely to be positive for the development of markets for private securities, portfolio diversification throughout the euro area and the integration of the capital markets. In principle, more integrated cash and capital markets were known to create markets for commercial paper and corporate securities in the euro area. A government loan based on Benchmark (reference value), increasing interest rates, less savings between letters and cash rates, lower costs to secure securities of private companies and increased competition in the issue sector are expected to represent positive incentives for companies to issue loans instead of loans in banks, thus attracting interest on interest rates and interest rates. In a long term, this will affect growth potential within the whole euro area. I am convinced that the efforts to integrate Europe in today's speech have not been made only with such economic and financial arguments to bring about the introduction of the single currency from three different perspectives, i.e. from a macro-economic perspective, from a microeconomic perspective and from a view of the financial market. However, I am convinced that the efforts to integrate Europe are not only with such economic and financial arguments. With this vision before your eyes, I can assure you that the ESF will take every effort to regain a smooth and successful start of the euro on 1 January 1999
